10965-the-world-turned-upside-down-or-no:
A small illustrated chapbook for children, this book turns the world upside down for laughs and learning. Each page pairs a plain fact with a strange reversal: seeing a butcher kill a hog is no news, but seeing a hare run after a dog is strange indeed. A tailor rides a goose, a rat builds a house, a dog plays the flute, and a lamb hunts a bear.

Roman and italic alphabets open the book, so children practise letters while enjoying the jokes. Pictures face the verses, showing cats fiddling while mice dance and horses playing chess. The chapbook belongs to early children's publishing, where nonsense taught reading and rewarded attention with surprise on every page.
11438-the-willows:
Algernon Blackwood's 1907 novella The Willows follows two travelers down the Danube between Vienna and Budapest. into a region of singular loneliness where the river spreads into marshes, painted Sümpfe on maps, covered by a vast sea of low willow bushes. The willows never become trees, remaining humble bushes swaying on slender stems, their silver leaves turning in wind waves like a sea. Channels, whirlpools, and foaming rapids tear at sandy banks.

Blackwood builds horror from landscape itself: the plain seems moving and alive, and the willows seem aware. The Willows is widely counted among the finest weird tales in English, influential and unsettling without monsters. Readers of supernatural fiction should start here for atmosphere over explanation.
13410-some-private-views:
James Payn gathers essays first printed in the Nineteenth Century and the Times, in a new edition of 1881 dedicated to Horace N. Pym. He writes on the midway inn, the critic on the hearth, sham admiration in literature, the pinch of poverty, story-telling, and penny fiction, then on hotels, maid-servants, men-servants, and whist players.

Payn claims his thoughts are not his own but the hidden common thought of all. A lady's hand crushed in a carriage door shows the pinch of poverty felt by birth and breeding, while Wilkie Collins's unknown public, readers by millions, waits to learn discrimination. The essays are chatty, observant, and mildly satirical about Victorian reading, service, and society.
14240-reviews:
Robert Ross edited this 1908 Methuen volume of Oscar Wilde's reviews, dedicating it to Mrs. Carew. Ross recalls eight years managing Wilde's literary property, with one friendship that annulled its disappointments. Dinners and Dishes opens the set, quoting Baudelaire: a man can live three days without bread but not one day without poetry. Pictures and music may lapse, Wilde insists, but poetry cannot.

Scottish and Australian letters fill the middle. Early Scots singers loved gardens, flowers, and birdsong, but not wild moorland, until Montgomerie wandered banks and braes and Drummond sang flood, forest, and hillside mist. Allan Ramsay, Thomson, and Beattie follow toward Wordsworth. Australian verse disappoints Wilde's reviewer: page after page of echoes without music, reflections without beauty, and magazine verse for colonial papers. Henry Clarence Kendall stands out as an exception. Criticism here stays witty, learned, and severe.
14282-a-merry-dialogue-declaringe-the-pr:
Desiderius Erasmus wrote this merry dialogue, printed in English in 1557, on shrewish wives and honest wives. Two women, Eulalia and Xantippa, talk over marriage, temper, and the art of living with a husband. Eulalia urges patience, good cheer, and a ready welcome at meeting. Xantippa answers with complaints of a beast of a husband. The text keeps the old spelling of its age, with its quaint forms and long sentences.

Eulalia holds that most husbands turn ill through their wives' own fault, and that a wife should never scold her man before company. She should speak her mind in private, then drop the matter and turn to pastime. Complaints, if they must be made, should go to his kin, not to strangers, and should blame the fault, not the man. The dialogue gives Tudor advice on wedlock: gentle rule, held tongues, and peace kept at home.
14531-the-singing-man-a-book-of-songs-an:
Josephine Preston Peabody's 1911 book of poems, published by Houghton Mifflin, gathers songs and shadows first printed in the Atlantic, Scribner's, and Harper's magazines. The contents run from The Singing Man to The Long Lane.

Peabody writes of trees, foundlings, feasters, golden shoes, and Paestum at noon, with a byway poem contrasting highway sun and byway despair. Her verse is lyrical and musical, with a touch of the Pre-Raphaelite. The collection shows a Boston poet of the early century at her most melodious, and it remains her best-known book.
14654-a-daughter-of-the-snows:
Jack London's A Daughter of the Snows, published in 1902 with illustrations by Frederick C. Yohn, follows Frona Welse in the Yukon gold rush. London had already written The Son of the Wolf and The Call of the Wild.

Frona arrives by steamer, hurrying because she was born in the big log-house between the pines and the river. She moves through a rough camp society of dances, waltzes, fur caps, and moose-skin moccasins. London makes her a strong, educated heroine who holds her own among miners and adventurers. The novel pairs northern adventure with a debate about what a woman may be.
16054-the-palace-of-darkened-windows:
An Eastern romance by Mary Hastings Bradley, author of The Favor of Kings, issued by D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1914. Edmund Frederick supplied the pictures. A frontispiece warns a girl in chapter four: there is no way out for her. Bradley dedicates the book to her husband. The palace of darkened windows holds the tale's mystery.

An eavesdropper, a captain's call, and a sorry quest lead within the palace walls. A girl in the bazaars, Billy's doubts, and a midnight visitor raise the stakes. A desperate game, a maid and a message, and a flight over the garden wall follow, with a girl from the harem and a rose room. The novel thrills as an Eastern adventure: veils, walls, and a rescue against the odds.
16398-what-necessity-knows:
L. Dougall's What Necessity Knows, published in New York by Longmans, Green in 1893 and inscribed to her brother John Redpath Dougall, draws on a childhood tradition of religious excitement. Its preface recalls the Millerite or Adventist stir of 1843. In one place a little band in white robes climbed a hill expecting the Second Advent. They then returned to be the laughing stock of neighbors. A child heard the tale as eccentricity, yet felt awe and pathos.

Dougall sets that picturesque event among gain-getting, market-driven neighbors, letting faith and commerce collide. The novel that follows tests belief, love, and necessity in a small community. Readers who like Victorian Canadian fiction will find a thoughtful, unusual story.
16729-lay-sermons-addresses-and-reviews:
Thomas Henry Huxley gathered these lay sermons, addresses, and reviews in 1870, issued by Macmillan in London. A prefatory letter to his friend Tyndall explains why the book has no formal dedication or preface. A grand lodge in front of cottages would look wrong. A full defense of old papers would mean writing a new one. The papers span years of his public work.

Huxley speaks as a man of science to a lay crowd, on nature, education, and the claims of faith and fact. His tone is bold, clear, and combative, with wit to match. The book gives a fine entry to Victorian science in public debate, and it shows Huxley as teacher, critic, and defender of free inquiry.
1750-laws:
Three old men walking the roads of Crete talk about founding a city from scratch, and the talk grows into Plato's longest work. Three old men — an Athenian, a Spartan, and a Cretan — walk and talk about founding a new city. They lay down its laws in detail: education, marriage, property, courts, and the worship of the gods.

Unlike the Republic, which imagines rule by philosophers, the Laws settles for second best: written law, mixed rule, and citizens trained by habit. Its genuineness is backed by Aristotle's many citations of it. Readers will find Plato at his most practical here, and also his most severe, as he tries to build a city that could actually stand.
1875-painted-windows:
Elia W. Peattie's Painted Windows invites the reader into the chamber of memory, to lift eyes to windows where figures and scenes of childhood appear. Peattie writes of her own past with kindly eyes, hoping that long wished-for visions of the reader's own will rise beside them.

The sketches that follow move through storms that carry the writer beyond excitement into exultation, where conceit and sulkiness die and she finds herself alive and loved. Peattie's prose is warm and reflective, and the book works as a memoir in fragments, each window lit by a moment that shaped a life.
18859-cross-purposes-and-the-shadows:
George MacDonald gathered two fairy tales in this volume: Cross Purposes and The Shadows. The first opens in Fairyland, where the queen, bored by her too-well-behaved subjects, longs for a mortal or two at court. Her courtier Peaseblossom offers to fetch a girl, opening the road before her and closing it behind her.

Both tales use fairy magic to test human character, with children and ordinary folk caught in enchantments that reveal their true selves. MacDonald's stories mix wonder with moral reflection, in the Victorian fairy-tale manner. Readers get two gentle, imaginative tales, suitable for reading aloud, from a writer much admired by later fantasy authors.
1922-deirdre-of-the-sorrows:
J. M. Synge's Deirdre of the Sorrows, his last play, retells the Irish legend of Deirdre. She is the girl fated to bring ruin to kings, and Naisi is the lover she runs away with. The persons of the play include Lavarcham, Deirdre's nurse, and Owen, a servant, and the acts move from Deirdre's youth to her flight and return.

Deirdre, grown to a queen, tells Naisi how she heard a voice singing in the woods at full moon, gathered up her skirts and ran on a little path she had found. Synge writes the legend in prose of great beauty, and the play's tragedy lies in its knowledge: Deirdre sees her fate clearly and walks toward it anyway.
19901-the-castle-of-the-shadows:
Mrs. C. N. Williamson wrote The Castle of the Shadows as a romance of Italy. Afternoon sunshine pours over its opening scene in a valley. Wooded hills shut the valley in on either side. Their rugged heads stay gilded while their shoulders fall into shadow. A girl's hair burns gold in that light. Two men watch her, and the watching matters. Williamson builds desire out of landscape.

The Williamsons' romances sold travel and love in one package. A castle of shadows promises secrets, pursuit, and a hidden past. Italian scenery does half their storytelling work. This novel follows their proven, popular pattern. Readers got a tour and a courtship together. It is Edwardian romance at full polish.
20447-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Robert G. Ingersoll was America's most famous lecturer against orthodox religion, and this eighth volume of his works gathers his interviews. Reporters asked him about the Bible, the church, and the afterlife. He answered in the plain, bold style that filled halls across the country.

Ingersoll says he regards the Bible, above all the Old Testament, as he does most other ancient books. In it he finds some truth, a great deal of error, considerable barbarism, and a most plentiful lack of good sense. The interviews preserve his wit and his case for free thought.
21657-deep-furrows:
Hopkins Moorhouse tells how prairie farmers built co-operatives in Deep Furrows, copyrighted in Canada in 1918. Wheatlands spread to the skyline around the Qu'Appelle trail in October 1901. A rider seems to hang still in the vast landscape as the tale opens.

The trail forks through the Qu'Appelle valley toward the Pheasant Hills and Fishing Lakes. Moorhouse frames the history as a tale of pioneer trails and hard fights. Farmers of western Canada won great feats in co-operation along those roads. Verse by E. Pauline Johnson, on the legend of Qu'Appelle, sets the book's elegiac tone.
22237-messages-from-the-epistle-to-the-h:
Messages from the Epistle to the Hebrews gathers the large spiritual lessons of that New Testament letter. The writer refuses two temptations at the start. He will not argue about who wrote Hebrews, and he will not expound it verse by verse in a few short chapters. Instead he takes the epistle as it stands, somewhat as a whole.

From it he draws conspicuous messages, as he calls them, of the Word that lives and abides forever. Faith, priesthood, sacrifice, and endurance are the letter's great themes. The book is devotional rather than critical, meant for Bible readers at home. It shows the preaching style that treated Hebrews as a storehouse of comfort for tired churches.
2705-sally-dows:
Bret Harte opens Sally Dows with a prologue on the last gun at Snake River, where a dewy country lane turns by noon into a scene of war's aftermath. The title story follows Sally herself, with the conspiracy of Mrs. Bunker and the transformation of Buckeye Camp.

Their uncle from California brings eastern money and western manners into collision. Harte writes of post war California with his usual mix of romance and irony, and Sally stands as one of his strongest heroines. The volume shows Harte's later craft, compact, humane, and quietly surprising.
27805-the-wind-in-the-willows:
Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows appears here in the 1913 Scribner's edition, illustrated by Paul Bransom, after a 1908 copyright. The story begins with Mole spring-cleaning his little home, then flinging down his brush and bolting out into spring.

Mole meets Rat, Badger, and the incorrigible Toad, and the chapters move from the river bank and the open road through the wild wood to Toad's adventures and the return of Ulysses. Gentle, funny, and lyrical, the book has become a classic of children's literature and of English pastoral imagination.
28763-imaginary-interviews:
William Dean Howells wrote this 1910 book of essays framed as conversations that never happened. The imaginary interviews take up New York life, Italian opera, vaudeville, magazines, travel, and the habits of rich and poor city folk. Extra essays treat autumn, letter writing, and advice from literary age to literary youth. Harper and Brothers published it in New York and London.

Howells uses the interview form to air opinions lightly: a niece advises her uncle on writing, a home-comer sizes up New York, and a grandfather talks about reading. The pieces are witty rather than angry, and they show a leading American novelist commenting on his own changing country. The book suits readers who like social observation done with humor and a light hand.
289-the-wind-in-the-willows:
Mole, tired of spring cleaning, meets Rat on the river bank and never looks back. Kenneth Grahame's Wind in the Willows follows Mole, Rat, Badger, and the reckless Toad through woods, roads, and river days. Toad's motorcar mania lands him in prison and his home in weasel hands.

Chapters like Dulce Domum, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, and Wayfarers All mix comedy with wonder. The animals' friendship, food, and fights feel deeply English and deeply human. Grahame wrote the tales for his son, and they grew into a classic. The book endures as a children's masterpiece.
29505-suggestions-to-the-jews:
Written by a Jew and printed in London by John Wertheimer and Company, this pamphlet offers suggestions to the Jews for improvement in reference to their charities, education, and general government. Its argument grows from hope and fear, from a sense of the community's own best interests and those of its posterity. Honor and reputation, the author says, must guide reform from within.

The pamphlet speaks as an insider to insiders, urging better organization of charity, schooling, and communal rule. Its tone is earnest and practical, not polemical. Students of Anglo-Jewish history will find a rare, early nineteenth-century voice on communal self-improvement, written before emancipation debates reshaped the question.
30193-east-of-the-shadows:
Mrs. Hubert Barclay, Edith Noël Barclay, sets a novel of love and choice in England, published at Toronto by Hodder and Stoughton in 1913. Chapters named Philippa, Phil, the stranger, Francis, Isabella, Doctor Gale, and indecision lead to the heart of Bessmoor, a square in the patchwork, the major's visit, and violets. Progress, threads, ropes of gossamer, and revelation follow, with hopes for the future, Isabella's point of view, and Marion speaking her mind.

The opening sends a train out of a terminus, its porter slamming a door, its engine snorting, its cars gliding through a maze of buildings. Philippa, courteous though coy and gentle though retired, carries the story's center, in the words of Crabbe quoted at her chapter head. Halcyon days, bitter-sweet hours, poor Rip, friendship, and content close a tale of hearts tested and settled.
31088-taxonomy-and-distribution-of-some-:
James S. Findley's 1955 paper tidies the taxonomy and ranges of several American shrews, published as volume 7, number 14 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. Two Ohio specimens long listed as the common cinereous shrew prove, on small size, short tails, and tooth form, to belong to the subspecies ohionensis. That pushes its known range about seventy miles south to Milford Center.

A Veracruz shrew earlier assigned to a Texas form is likewise shown to be Cryptotis micrura on comparison with specimens from northern Veracruz and southern Tamaulipas. Short and specimen-based, the paper shows museum taxonomy at work, correcting names one skin and skull at a time.
31715-a-prince-of-good-fellows:
Robert Barr's Prince of Good Fellows, illustrated by Edmund J. Sullivan, was published at New York by McClure, Phillips, and Company in May 1902, with copyright in 1901 and 1902. Its eleven stories follow a king through a round of adventures, and their titles tell the course: the king intervenes, dines, keeps a tryst, and investigates. Then come the king's gold, the king a-begging, and the king's visit.

The king explores, drinks, sails, and at last weds, closing a sequence of courtly comedy and adventure. Barr's stories are light, gallant, and good-humored, and they show a prince who meets the world on its own terms.
32116-when-the-cock-crows:
Waldron Baily's adventure novel, published in New York by the Bedford Publishing Company in 1918 with drawings by G. W. Gage, is a coastal tale built around a man named Ichabod. Baily had earlier written Heart of the Blue Ridge and The Homeward Trail. He dedicated this book to Josephus Daniels, praised for courage, determination, and achievement in a great crisis. Its contents promise island life, storms, and a hero's slow awakening.

The chapters run from Ichabod's Island and Among the Breakers, through a new calamity, a prisoner of morphia, and a hunt for a clue, to stormbound days and eyes from the deep. Later chapters give the awakening of Ichabod, scenes among fisherfolk, Garnet the hero, and an episode adrift with a madman, before a coming-out party closes the list. Readers get a period sea-coast romance, mixing mystery, danger, and a community bound to the water.
32968-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistle-:
Thomas Charles Edwards, principal of the University College of Wales, wrote this volume on the Epistle to the Hebrews for the Expositor's Bible series, edited by W. Robertson Nicoll and published in London in 1904. Edwards works through the letter passage by passage, explaining its argument about Christ, priesthood, sacrifice, and faith for preachers and general readers rather than for specialists alone.

The commentary treats Hebrews as a careful, sustained piece of reasoning, not a loose set of sayings, and it tries to show how each part serves the whole. Edwards's tone is learned but pastoral, aiming to help a reader preach or study the text with confidence. As a work of Edwardian biblical exposition, it remains a clear guide to one of the New Testament's hardest letters.
32997-the-style-book-of-the-detroit-news:
The Style Book of the Detroit News gathers the rules that governed writing and editing at one of Michigan's leading papers. Its editor drew on government and university style books and on standard works on newspaper writing, with permission to adapt a digest of New York libel law to Michigan. Inscriptions on the newspaper's building, written by Professor Fred N. Scott of Michigan, appear in boxes.

The book also records the paper's own history, founded by James Edmund Scripps in 1873, with a Sunday edition from 1884. As a style book, it shows what editors valued: clear spelling, consistent usage, and care with law and libel. For journalists and historians of the press, it is a compact window on how a great city daily taught its staff to write fairly and well.
33112-shapes-and-shadows:
Madison Cawein's Shapes and Shadows gathers poems that move from nature and memory to love, art, and the nation's wars. Its contents run from The Evanescent Beautiful and August through The Higher Brotherhood, Gramarye, and Dreams. They go on to The Old House, The Rock, and Rain, then on to Standing-Stone Creek, The Moonmen, and The Old Man Dreams. Later poems include Tristram and Isolt, Dusk in the Woods, At the Ferry, and a southern girl and a daughter of the states.

An opening patriotic poem under the stars and stripes, urging sons to uphold the name their fathers blazoned, shows Cawein's public voice beside his private lyrics. The collection's dedication speaks of bards of old and the flame that fell on them, and Cawein's own verse aims for musical beauty and feeling. It is a representative volume from a Kentucky poet once widely read.
35258-contagious-abortion-of-cows:
MacNeal, a bacteriologist at the University of Illinois, wrote Contagious Abortion of Cows with Herbert Mumford, chief in animal husbandry. It appeared as Bulletin 152 of the Agricultural Experiment Station at Urbana in November 1911. The summary states the case plainly. A specific contagious disease causing abortion in cows has long been known abroad, and it is certain that the same disease prevails in the United States.

The germ, the bulletin says, was first described by the Danish investigators Bang and Stribolt, and the station found it in afterbirths from aborting cows. The cure is a regime. Isolate the affected cows and cleanse them with antiseptic until discharge ceases. Burn all infectious material, disinfect the stalls, and treat the herd bull before and after service, with a clean bull kept for heifers. The bulletin turns laboratory proof into farm orders, in the plain style of the experiment station press.
35302-the-genial-idiot-his-views-and-rev:
The Genial Idiot: His Views and Reviews is a humour book by John Kendrick Bangs, published by Harper and Brothers in 1908. Bangs also wrote A House-Boat on the Styx and Coffee and Repartce. The Idiot of his comic pieces is a boarding-house talker whose foolish remarks carry sharp sense. His views and reviews gather his talk on books, plays, and the news of the day.

Bangs was a leading American humorist of his time, an editor as well as a writer. This volume collects pieces in his best-known vein: light satire spoken by a cheerful fool. The catalogue of his books in the front matter shows how steady the demand for them ran.
35426-polaris-of-the-snows:
Charles B Stilson wrote Polaris of the Snows for the All-Story Cavalier in December nineteen fifteen. The Munsey company held the copyright. A dying old man opens the tale with a cry. North, north, to the north, Polaris, he gasps: tell the world, you must go.

Throwing off the covers, the giant rises tottering from his low couch. His eyes glaze and his voice chokes to a hoarse rattle. One last rally lifts his arm to point north before he falls like a tree. His companion closes his eyes with light, sure fingers. Polaris, who has never seen a human being die, sits down utterly alone. A deathbed charge launches the arctic tale.
35695-the-allied-countries-and-the-jews:
A set of wartime addresses by Rabbi H G Enelow of Temple Emanu-El, New York. The addresses were delivered in the autumn of 1917. A publisher issued them in book form in 1918. Six countries receive one address each. France, England, Russia, and Italy come first. Palestine and America complete the survey. A seventh address looks to the war's end and the Jewish future.

Enelow opens with France and its Jewish history. American sons, he notes, will soon fight on French soil. American women already serve there in relief work. The series traces emancipation and loyalty country by country. Russia's revolution had just changed its Jewish question entirely. The book captures American Jewish thought in the First World War's last full year.
35904-the-five-arrows:
The Five Arrows, by Allan Chase, is a novel of wartime Puerto Rico intrigue. Random House issued it at New York, its rights never renewed, a note says. Ground batteries over San Juan bay fire at a target plane in chapter one. Guests at La Fortaleza watch tracers chase the silver sleeve in the sky.

Pearl Harbor talk and submarine net jokes set the island wartime mood early. A phone call summons Matthew Hall from the terrace into the plot. Hall walks with a steel spring tread, braced for floors to blow up. Paris in the thirties first marked that walk in him, friends noticed there. Espionage and sabotage fears drive this Caribbean thriller.
36798-the-limits-of-atheism-or-why-shoul:
George Jacob Holyoake's The Limits of Atheism, or Why Should Sceptics Be Outlaws, was printed in London in 1874 by Brook of the Strand, price twopence. The pages are inscribed to Richard William Jelf, principal of King's College, London. They are written, the dedication says, in arrest of the parliamentary judgment that places the word of the atheist below that of the felon. A sentence from Mill's On Liberty heads the pamphlet.

The preface is plain about its object: not to defend the intellectual accuracy of atheism, which so short a space forbids. Its object is to explain its case, vindicate its moral rectitude, and claim legal equality for those who hold it. Two atheisms, Holyoake argues, live in the literature: the ancient one of mere negation, and the affirmative form whose proper name is Cosmism, illustrated by Humboldt and expounded by Comte.
37424-views-and-reviews:
Henry James's early criticism fills this collection, printed by Ball at Boston in 1908 and now first gathered. Phillips, who compiled a bibliography of James, brought the pieces together. James wrote the first of them at twenty-three, on the novels of George Eliot, for the Atlantic in 1866.

Browning's drama, Swinburne's essays, and the poetry of William Morris follow. Arnold, Whitman, and Dickens each get a young critic's measure. Tennyson's Queen Mary and Harold are weighed act by act. The Whistler and Ruskin libel suit earns two sharp notes. Kipling's early stories close the book. James is already James here: patient, exacting, and sure that the critic's first duty is to find the author's ruling theory. The reviews are a great novelist's apprenticeship in public.
38120-bridge-axioms-and-laws:
Bridge Axioms and Laws is a guide to the card game of bridge by Elwell, revised to cover a change in the rules called the suit call. It was published in New York by Dutton in 1907. Elwell had written several bridge books before it, on the game in general, on advanced play, and on tournament hands.

The axioms stand at the front as short, sharp maxims. The best players, one says, are those who can draw sound inferences swiftly. Observation is an art that finds what other people's play both hides and shows. One inference leads to another, and each card played speaks through its silence. To talk with sense through the cards, a player must watch each one as it falls. The laws follow, giving the formal rules under the new call.
38327-the-history-of-sabatai-sevi-the-su:
John Evelyn wrote The History of Sabatai Sevi in 1669. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued it in 1968. Christopher W Grose wrote its intro. The Clark Memorial Library issued the reprint. It stands as Publication Number 131 of the line. Sevi was the supposed messiah of the Jews.

Evelyn's piece forms the weightiest part of another work. The History of the Three Late Famous Impostors holds it. Readers find it fascinating if unoriginal, Grose says. It adds to the great diarist's known work there. George Guffey and Maximillian Novak edited the line. Scholars from Michigan to London advised it. Robert Vosper of the Clark Library joins them. A diarist's tract on a false messiah shows how news of a Jewish prophet-king stirred London in the year of plague's aftermath.
38635-delilah-of-the-snows:
Harold Bindloss wrote Delilah of the Snows, a novel of the Canadian North published by Frederick A Stokes of New York. The copyright dates to 1907, and this printing to May 1908. Bindloss also wrote Alton of Somasco and Winston of the Prairie. His hero, Walter Ingleby, first appears at an English tennis match, swinging his racket by a hazel hedge.

The chapters quickly move Ingleby to a new country of trails and snow. Hetty bears the cost of his choices, one title says. A trooper named Probyn meets misadventure, and a man named Sewell falls. A blockade and a snowed-in camp raise the stakes near the end. Bindloss sets questions of duty and failure against gold-country cold.
38749-our-house-and-london-out-of-our-wi:
Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote this portrait of a London household, printed by Houghton Mifflin in 1912. Her husband Joseph Pennell drew the views: barges at Waterloo Bridge, gulls in winter flight, and Cleopatra's Needle from their windows. The Thames flows past every chapter.

The book is peopled by servants. Henrietta, Trimmer, and Louise arrive in turn; charwomen, an old housekeeper, and a new one follow. Beggars and tenants get chapters of their own. The quarter closes the tour. A foreigner in London, Pennell learned that an Englishman's house is his castle only when run on approved lines. Her comedy is gentle and exact. The Pennells made London their subject for years, and this is among their most intimate books.
39596-georgina-of-the-rainbows:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote Georgina of the Rainbows, issued in New York by the Britton Publishing Company with copyright in nineteen sixteen. Johnston had earlier written Two Little Knights of Kentucky. She dedicated the book to her little god daughter Anne Elizabeth. Twenty two chapters fill the tale, set at the tip of old Cape Cod.

Her Earlier Memories opens the story. Georgina Playmate Mother and The Towncrier Has His Say follow. New Friends and the Green Stairs and In the Footsteps of Pirates come next. The Tishbite and The Telegram That Took Barby Away fill the early chapters. The Birthday Prism and Moving Pictures stand in the middle. The Old Rifle Gives Up Its Secret and Buried Treasure raise the hunt. Girls get a Cape Cod summer of rainbows and buried treasure.
40663-two-on-the-trail-a-story-of-canada:
Nell, fifteen, and her brother David, twelve, are alone in a log house in the Canadian snows when their father fails to come home. Cowper's story, published by the Sheldon Press in 1922, follows the two through the wait and the search, with winter closing in and a wolf's howl carrying across the trees. David, called Da, looks to his sister, and Nell has to be braver than her years.

The book is a tale of endurance for young readers, built on plain dangers: cold, hunger, wild animals, and the fear that their father is lost for good. The children's care for each other carries the story more than any single adventure. Snow, trail, and cabin are drawn from the northern life Cowper knew and wrote about often.
42973-the-house-of-the-white-shadows:
B L Farjeon wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1903 and published at New York in 1904 by R F Fenno. The American edition opens with sad news: since the book went to press, its author had died in London at the age of seventy.

A short life of Farjeon stands before the story. Born in London in 1833, he went out young to Australia and then to New Zealand, where he ran a newspaper venture at Dunedin. Home again, he launched his first novel in London in 1870, Grif, a story of Australian life, and its success fixed his career. More than twenty-five works of fiction followed.
44574-the-missouri-outlaws:
The Missouri Outlaws is a western tale by Gustave Aimard. Percy St John turned the French text into English for this print. The book came out in London in the year eighteen seventy seven. A front note tells the strange true life of the man who wrote it.

Aimard was raised as a son of a great tribe of the plains, it says. He lived with them past fifteen years, with gun and axe in hand. Squatter, trapper, chief hand, and gold digger mark his wild road west. The tale that follows then claims the truth of a life lived so. Ship scenes and kin advice open the chain of outlaw deeds.
4554-lovers-vows:
Mrs. Inchbald adapted this play in five acts from the German of Kotzebue, and it is set in Germany over a single day. The action moves between a small inn, a cottage, a castle, and a prison tower, following Baron Wildenhaim, Count Cassel, Anhalt, Frederick, and the women around them, Agatha Firburg and Amelia Wildenhaim. A prologue and epilogue frame the drama, which was written for the stage with named actors in mind.

At its heart lies a story of seduction, family duty, and forgiveness, as old wrongs surface and young lovers press their claims. Inchbald keeps the pace brisk, shifting scenes between high road, cottage room, and castle chamber. Readers get a lively late Georgian drama about honour, rank, and second chances, best read aloud or imagined on stage, where each act tightens the knot before it is cut.
45657-the-camp-fire-girls-amid-the-snows:
Margaret Vandercook sent her Camp Fire Girls into a New Hampshire winter in this 1913 volume. A December storm in those hills is a serious thing, the first chapter warns. Through it, two girls travel a rough road between cedar and pine, laughing and singing as sleigh bells ring. Their goal is Sunrise Cabin, where the group will spend the season.

The chapters promise Christmas Eve at the cabin, a Camp Fire play, an Indian love song, and the story of a black sheep brought back into the fold. Vandercook wrote whole series for girls, the Ranch Girls and the Red Cross Girls among them. These tales mixed outdoor life, friendship, and small moral trials, and they found eager readers in the years when the Camp Fire movement itself was new.
4594-home-lights-and-shadows:
T. S. Arthur published Home Lights and Shadows at New York in 1853, gathering short domestic sketches under one moral idea. His preface says that love makes the home-lights and selfishness the shadows, and that few people never darken, for a time, the homes that should grow bright at their coming. The contents include Rights and Wrongs, The Humbled Pharisee, and Romance and Reality. They go on to Both to Blame, The Mother's Promise, The Two Husbands, and Visiting as Neighbors.

Later sketches cover a dollar on the conscience, helping the poor, following the fashions, and making a sensation, among other homely cases. Each piece is short, plain, and aimed at conduct in family life. Readers get a typical mid-century American gift book of moral tales, easy to dip into story by story. It is a clear window into what Victorian households were taught to praise and to avoid.
4766-windows:
John Galsworthy wrote Windows as a play in the fifth series of his plays, set in Geoffrey March's house at Highgate in springtime. Its persons include Geoffrey March, his wife Joan, and their children Mary and Johnny. Their cook, Mr. Bly, their window cleaner, and his daughter Faith Bly also appear, with Blunter, a strange young man, and Mr. Barnadas.

Act one opens on a Thursday morning in the dining-room after breakfast. Act two follows a fortnight later after lunch, and act three the same day after dinner. The dining-room opens through French windows onto a garden that seems infinite, till side walls show it finite at the far end, where acacias and sumachs screen another house. French and other windows form all the outer wall. Readers get a tense Galsworthy play about a household, a stranger, and what windows reveal and hide.
50556-the-jews:
The Jews is Hilaire Belloc's study of the Jewish presence in European society, first published by Constable and Company of London in 1922. Belloc dedicated the book to Miss Ruby Goldsmith, his secretary for many years at King's Land and, in his words, the best and most intimate of his family's Jewish friends.

His first chapter states the thesis plainly. The Jews are an alien body within the society they inhabit, and from that fact, he argues, irritation and friction arise, so a problem exists whose solution is urgently necessary. The contents summary holds that such a body is dealt with by elimination or by exclusion in its several forms, or else by recognition. Whatever a reader's verdict, the book is a fixed point in the debate of its decade and cannot be skipped in studying it.
53995-a-study-in-shadows:
William Locke wrote A Study in Shadows, printed in London in 1908 by John Lane. Chapter one, The Lone Women, opens with Felicia Graves at the Pension Boccard. Six weeks there had confused many of her conceptions and brought things before her judgment for which her standards were too small. She had passed her young womanhood in the bubbling life of a garrison town, not in village innocence.

Locke sets his sheltered heroine among the exiles and adventurers of a foreign pension, where every guest casts a shadow. Love and self knowledge grow in that shaded air. Locke writes with his usual grace and gentle irony. Readers get a fine, quiet novel of a girl learning the world at a Swiss table.
5654-what-every-woman-knows:
James M. Barrie wrote What Every Woman Knows as a comedy opening in a little Scotch room, where James Wylie is about to move on the draughtboard amid an awful silence befitting the occasion. With his hand poised, since touching a piece means playing it, James raises his red head to read his father Alick's face. Alick pretends panic lest James make this move, then is caught in unholy ecstasy as James grins.

The play follows Maggie Wylie and John Shand, asking what a woman knows and what a man owes her wit. Barrie writes Scottish family comedy with tenderness. Readers get a beloved stage comedy about marriage, ambition, and the quiet power behind success.
56850-the-night-the-mountain-fell-the-st:
The Night the Mountain Fell is a book by Edmund Christopherson about the Montana Yellowstone earthquake. It was printed by Yellowstone Publications of West Yellowstone, Montana, with copyright in 1960 and 1962. The book is offered to all who lived through the quake: those who suffered, those who helped, and those who were lost. Its chapters bear plain names such as Real Shook, Trapped, Outside World, First Patrol and Rescue.

Later chapters cover the puzzle faced by the civil defence men, the freeing of those trapped, and the question of who was hit. The book then turns to civil defence and natural disasters in general, the aftermath, and the living geology of the region. A last chapter tells readers what can now be seen at the site. Maps and drawings by DeLynn Colvert fill the book.
57239-japanese-plays-and-playfellows:
Osman Edwards wrote Japanese Plays and Playfellows, for Lane in 1901. Twelve coloured plates by Japanese artists fill the volume. Edwards gives the book to Lafcadio Hearn, poet and friend, with gratitude. A plate shows Benkei at sea, from the No drama of Japan. His preface owns that critics may resent his incense for Japan.

The musume, the Japanese girl, sums up much of her country's magic, he holds. Its picturesqueness, kindness, and politeness live in her dainty person, he says. On anti-foreign feeling he dwells at some length in the book. The witchery of Japan often hides unpleasant facts from fond visitors, he warns. He will not let his own pleasant souvenirs suppress that testimony. Edwards gives the theatre and the people of Japan together. The book mixes plays, players, and the playfellows round them.
5895-the-honor-of-the-big-snows:
James Oliver Curwood opens The Honor of the Big Snows at a bedside in the north woods, where a woman whispers to John that she hears music. Her white, thin hand lifts weakly to the rough face of the man kneeling beside her bed. Her great dark eyes grow luminously bright for a moment. She whispers again that she hears music. A sigh follows, and the chapter, called The Music, sets the novel's tone.

The tale follows a story of the Canadian snow country, where honor, love, and survival are tested by cold and distance. Curwood writes with vivid northern atmosphere, favoring emotion and adventure over subtlety. The book suits readers of wilderness romance, and fans of Curwood's tales of Mounties, trappers, and the big snows themselves.
60173-russia-in-the-shadows:
Russia in the Shadows is a work of reportage by Wells, published by George Doran of New York in 1921. Its frontispiece shows a Petersburg street on the site of a demolished wooden house. The chapters begin with Petersburg in Collapse and Drift and Salvage. The Quintessence of Bolshevism and The Creative Effort in Russia follow. The Petersburg Soviet is described as a legislative mass meeting.

The Dreamer in the Kremlin is his interview with Lenin; a plate shows the two men in conversation. Photographs also show Gorky among a great dump of art, and the statue of Marx outside the Smolny. A passage preserved in the copy tells how the trip came about. In 1914 Wells had visited Petersburg and Moscow for a couple of weeks. In September 1920 he was asked to repeat the visit by the Russian Trade Delegation in London.
60362-dark-windows:
A science fiction story by Bryce Walton. Worlds of If Science Fiction printed it in October 1957. The narrator wakes at dawn in a chilled room. Through the thin wall he hears a cry of pain. His neighbour Donnicker, an old shoemaker, falls heavily. Men load the body into a black car. A broadcast voice then assures all citizens. The past is dead, it says, and today everyone is safe.

The narrator comforts himself with a cold logic. Donnicker must have hidden something. His own clearance is clean. Safety lies in knowing nobody and seeing nothing. The story builds dread from that obedience. Rusting tractors and hand ploughs fill the news. A watched society smiles from every screen.
61102-the-valley-of-squinting-windows:
Brinsley Macnamara wrote The Valley of the Squinting Windows, copyrighted in 1919 and published at New York in 1920 by Brentano's. The catalog dates it 1919 and keeps the closing words. Macnamara dedicated the story to one who waited for it. A text from Leviticus on blemish fronts the book darkly.

The prefatory note opens in a parlor, and the valley of the title closes around its people. Macnamara's Irish midland town watches itself through windows that squint with suspicion, envy, and spite. The novel caused a storm in Ireland: his own district knew itself in the valley, and the book was burned and its author boycotted. It remains a fierce classic of Irish small town life. The squinting windows are the eyes of neighbors who miss nothing and forgive less.
61661-circular-saws:
Humbert Wolfe wrote Circular Saws, a book of very short tales printed in London in 1923. A few of them had run in weekly papers before. Wolfe was also a poet, author of a book of London sonnets.

Each tale takes a proverb for its title and its theme. The contents run from "Waste not, want not" through "All's well that ends well" and "Silence is golden" to "Look before you leap." Some titles are Latin tags instead. The tales are brief, most only a page or two, and each turns its saying over to show a fresh side. Wolfe's light touch made the book a pleasant sample of the short prose sketches popular between the wars.
62012-a-week-in-wall-street-by-one-who-k:
A writer who signs as One Who Knows wrote a short book on Wall Street. The book came out in New York in 1841. It claims to show a week in the stock trade from the inside. An early note deals with the old city wall that gave the street its name. Frederick Jackson filed the rights that year.

First chapters tell how joint stock firms and brokers arose. A tale of the Morrison Kennel works in a stock scheme. Later parts show how stocks are bought and sold. The United States Bank plays a part in the tale. Readers get an early, sharp view of the trade.
63868-the-boy-miners-or-the-enchanted-is:
The Boy Miners, or The Enchanted Island, is a dime novel by Edward Ellis. Its subtitle calls it a tale of the Yellowstone country. Beadle and Adams published it in New York. The copyright was entered in the year 1874. The contents list fifteen chapters of adventure. The first chapter is titled There They Come in bold style. Young Edwin Inwood opens the tale on watch in a tree. He has been perched there for half an hour.

Edwin leaps down and runs to a brook in alarm. His elder brother George and a man named Jim Tubbs wait there. They raise their heads, looking toward the sentinel boy. George catches up his shovel and his rifle at once. His question, how many are there, hangs over the scene. The tale promises boy miners, danger, and a strange island. It is a frontier adventure built for the dime novel market.
65455-chinese-vs-negroes-as-american-cit:
Scottron, a member of the school board in Brooklyn and a well known Black citizen there, set out his views in this pamphlet on Chinese and Black Americans as citizens. The piece centers on a letter he wrote to the Brooklyn Eagle. It takes up a plan for settling Black Americans in South America.

Scottron answers a writer who had assumed the government would go on using Asian labor in its new Pacific lands. He argues that Black Americans have qualities that fit them to be readily taken into the body politic. The pamphlet prints his letter and the paper that followed it as an interesting discussion. It preserves a Black civic leader's voice in a debate of his time.
66809-survival-at-altitude-for-heavy-and:
Restricted notes on the use of oxygen equipment in the B-17, B-24, and B-29 were issued in 1944 for combat crews. The information could be given to any person known to be in the service of the United States, the regulation quoted says. It could also go to persons of undoubted loyalty cooperating in government work, but not to the public or the press.

An index leads the manual: auto mix, the effect of oxygen on ceiling, dangers with oxygen, and the demand oxygen system. Demand type masks, duration of oxygen supply for the B-17 and B-24, the method of computing it, the emergency valve, and explosive decompression follow. Through long hours of tiring training you have developed superior judgment, the text tells crews. Most of that training was confined to relatively safe altitudes. High, thin air could kill a gunner quietly, and this book was written to stop it.
67775-the-lone-swallows:
Henry Williamson gathered his nature essays in The Lone Swallows, published in London in 1922. Most of the papers appear here for the first time; a few had run in newspapers and field magazines. A line from Richard Jefferies heads the book, asking readers to be tender to swallows.

Williamson's note thanks the editors who first printed his early work and encouraged him. He includes his first attempt at nature writing, called Winter's Eve, for reasons of sentiment. The essays describe the common sights and sounds of the English countryside with a young man's close eye. Williamson later won fame for Tarka the Otter; here readers see the apprentice learning his craft in the fields of Devon.
70570-red-shadows:
Red Shadows is a tale by Robert Howard, printed in Weird Tales in August 1928. It opens under a hazy moon, in a wild and threatening country where death might lurk under the trees. A tall wanderer with a long, slim rapier walks the valley, unhurried and unswerving, until a sound in the shadows stops him.

He finds not a foe but a wounded girl, her face like a dim white rose in the dark. She gasps out her tale: Le Loup and his men fell on her village, robbed, slew, and burned. The wanderer, Solomon Kane by the tale's own later talk, takes up her cause. Howard gives pulp readers a grim avenger in a haunted borderland.
71342-the-history-of-the-jews:
The History of the Jews is a concise history by Gotthard Deutsch, professor of history at Hebrew Union College. Bloch Publishing Company issued it in New York in 1910. Its eight chapters begin with the Babylonian Captivity in 586 before Christ and end with the period of emancipation from 1791. The era of the Talmud, the rise of Islam, and the era of the Crusades fill the middle.

Later chapters treat the Jews of Europe from 1040 to 1215, a period of oppression to 1492, and a period of improvement to 1791. Each era adds its religious history, literary activity, and spiritual life. A passage preserved in the copy marks a turning point. In 539, Cyrus, king of Persia, captured Babylon and became master of the whole Babylonian empire, and so of Palestine. He was favourably inclined to the Jews.
73710-my-study-windows:
James Russell Lowell wrote My Study Windows, a book of essays published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston. The copyright was entered in 1871, and this edition renews it in 1899 under his daughter's name. His prefatory note is a piece of self mockery. His former volume of essays, he says, was so kindly received that he is emboldened to make another, more mixed collection.

The papers here were written at intervals during the last fifteen years. He knew no way so effectual to rid his mind of them, he confesses, as shutting them between two covers where they can haunt him no more. He would have preferred a simpler title, but publishers nowadays are inexorable on that point. Lowell's windows looked out on Chaucer, Dryden, and the New England of his youth, and the essays remain the pleasantest of his prose.
74088-famous-funny-fellows:
Will Clemens published Famous Funny Fellows at Cleveland in 1882, a set of brief life sketches of American humorists. More than thirty names fill the contents. Samuel Clemens, called Mark Twain, leads the list, and no kinship beyond the name need be read into the honour. Artemus Ward, Josh Billings, Bill Nye, and Eugene Field all have their chapters.

Uncle Remus's creator, Joel Chandler Harris, stands beside Petroleum Nasby and Bill Arp. Clemens writes of the dialect and newspaper school of American fun, men whose sketches ran in the daily press and made whole regions laugh. In his opening he notes how new the trade was: a score of years before, the country's humorists could be counted on one hand. The book is a group portrait of the first great age of American comic writing, taken while many of its stars still lived.
74230-nantucket-windows:
Edwina Stanton Babcock wrote verses of Nantucket island life and light. The Inquirer and Mirror Press issued Nantucket Windows on the island in 1924. Some poems first ran in The National Magazine and island papers. The book is given to Annie Barker Folger for her fireside welcome.

Island windows glimmer gold on the moors in the title poem's opening. Ghost houses, docks, lightships, and the town clock fill the contents in turn. Poems honor Maria Mitchell and Abram Quary, the last Indian on Nantucket. Readers gain a tender, close portrait of an island in verse.
74243-many-furrows:
Many Furrows is a book of familiar essays by Alpha of the Plough, published by Dent. The pen name hides Alfred George Gardiner, the journalist. The book first appeared in 1924; this is the Wayfarer's Library issue of 1927. Gardiner dedicates it to his wife. Some fifty short essays fill the contents. Dream Journeys opens the volume with a castaway fantasy.

Gardiner dreams himself into Robinson Crusoe's place on the island. Stores of potatoes lie about, and no rescue is wanted for many a day. The essays that follow treat small occasions in the same easy voice. Saying please, shaking hands, shop windows, and unposted letters all get their pieces. A day with the bees and the case of Dean Inge widen the range. The Unknown Warrior and naming the baby turn grave and tender.
74969-marionettes-masks-and-shadows:
Winifred Mills and Louise Dunn wrote a craft book on puppets, masks, and shadow plays. The book came out in New York in 1927. Mills led art work at a Cleveland school. Dunn worked in art teaching at the Cleveland Museum of Art. Corydon Bell drew the pictures.

One part traces the string puppet's kin and famed friends. It then teaches how to pick a play, build a stage, and make the dolls. Scenery, props, lights, and crew drill fill the rest of that part. Mask and shadow parts come next with the same plain steps. Teachers and clubs get a full kit for stage craft.
75324-the-early-history-of-the-hebrews:
The Early History of the Hebrews retells the Bible's first ages in the light of new learning. Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, wrote the book. Rivingtons published it at London in 1897. A list of contents promises patriarchs, Moses, and the settlement in Canaan.

Sayce opens by asking who the Hebrews were and whence the name came. Ur and its kings, Harran, and the Amorites set the scene. Abraham's move to Canaan is matched against Babylonian records. Amraphel is weighed as the great law king Hammurabi. Sodom, Melchizedek, and the purchase of Machpelah each get treatment. A second chapter asks how the first five books were put together. Sayce writes for Bible readers who wanted the monuments to speak.
76288-the-city-without-jews:
The City Without Jews, subtitled A Novel of Our Time, is Hugo Bettauer's satire of Vienna. Brainin translated it from the German, in an authorized English version. Bloch printed it in New York in 1927.

The first chapter is named for its premise: the anti-Jewish law. A crowd walls the Parliament Building from the University to the Bellaria. All Vienna packs the June morning to watch. Later heads trace the law's working out in homes and shops. A shot, closing time, and a middle-class Viennese home fill the first part. Letters to Paris, bankrupt shops, and the end of the tenants' law fill the second. The League of True Christians and a stormy debate raise the heat. The tale ends where it must: the repeal of the law, and a cry of my beloved Jew.
76294-sparrows:
Sparrows, novelized by Marie Coolidge-Rask from a story by Winifred Dunn, retells a Mary Pickford film. Grosset and Dunlap published the book at New York in 1926. Scenes from the photoplay illustrate the volume throughout its pages. A front plate shows a threat that none of the kids get any supper.

Chapter one is a cry for help, and the home of the monster follows. Maria finds a companion, and an unequal struggle marks the early plot. Banishment, new victims, and a missing Buddy raise the stakes in the contents. A reign of terror, plotters, and a kidnapping carry the tale toward its climax. Crossing the bog and ransom money close the chase in the later chapters. Child waifs on a southern farm give the film tale its tears and thrills.
76901-birth-control-laws:
Mary Ware Dennett wrote Birth Control Laws: Shall We Keep Them, Change Them, or Abolish Them, issued in New York in nineteen twenty-six. The Grafton Press published her argument. Dennett was a founder of the National Birth Control League. She had directed the Voluntary Parenthood League and written The Sex Side of Life.

Part one asks what sort of laws America now has. Not even parents, she notes, can lawfully tell married children how to space their babies. No doctor can lawfully study the control of conception in full. Dennett walks through the federal acts and the state laws one by one. Clinics under those laws get their own hard look. Her title asks the reader to judge.
76914-the-mystery-of-the-missing-eyebrow:
Stephen Rudd wrote The Mystery of the Missing Eyebrows as the first of twelve books about newspaper boys. The Gore Publishing Company issued it in 1921 in the Newspaper Boys' Series. Its hero, Renfro Horn, was a real newspaper carrier, the author explains, whose likeness stands in the book. The stories were meant to teach carriers their responsibility to the world.

The frontispiece shows Renfro at work on the mystery. His hand trembles as he slips a warmed knife blade under a frozen eyebrow on a window pane and lifts it off. A notebook comes from his pocket next. Other Renfro Horn stories listed here include The Mystery of the Blue Milk and The Luck of a Rainy Night. The series turned the paper route into detection and adventure.
77027-a-brief-summary-in-plain-language-:
Barbara Leigh Smith wrote a brief summary in plain language of the most important laws concerning women, in a second edition printed at London in 1856 and sold for threepence. A single woman, Smith begins, has the same rights to property and protection, and pays the same taxes, as a man. Yet a woman of twenty one with the property qualification cannot vote for members of Parliament.

She can vote on parish questions, Smith notes. The pamphlet then treats married women's legal condition, where rights shrank sharply. Smith, later Barbara Bodichon, led the campaign that produced this summary. It armed the first organized English feminists with exact law.
77035-liberty-and-the-news:
Liberty and the News is a tract on the press by Walter Lippmann. Harcourt published the book at New York in 1920. Two of its essays first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly. Lippmann opens by praising the long editorship of the Manchester Guardian as a model for the trade.

The contents hold three essays on the bond between free government and true news. The first reaches back to the first American newspaper of 1690. That paper was shut down after one issue for printing high reflections. Its prospectus had promised to print only what the editor had reason to believe true. It also promised to correct mistakes in the next number. Lippmann takes that old pledge as the higher law of journalism. The essays argue that liberty fails when the news fails.
77378-poison-shadows:
William Le Queux wrote a mystery issued in New York, with rights held in 1927. The Macaulay Company brought out Poison Shadows, first known in England as The Chameleon. Thirty-three chapters run from A Soul for Sale to a close. Le Queux had written The Tattoo Mystery, as the title page notes.

At a Belgian coast hotel, Lady Wyndcliffe plots with the hunchback Gordon Routh. They mean to wed his ward Sibell to rich Gussie Gretton for his cash. Poor young doctor Otway, whom Sibell loves, must be cleared from their path. Greed, lies, and hidden foes drive a fast tale of plots and peril.
77570-women-in-the-shadows:
Ann Bannon wrote Women in the Shadows, an original Gold Medal novel published by Fawcett in 1959. All its characters, the copyright page insists, are fictional. The story is told in part through a diary. Its writer, Laura, opens on June 8, the second anniversary of her life with Beebo.

The anniversary party, Laura writes, felt more like a wake, with the corpse of a romance in the middle of the room. Jack, a friend, got terribly drunk as usual. Laura keeps her diary locked in a steel strongbox in the closet. She writes only when alone, before Beebo comes home from work. Bannon wrote frankly about women loving women for the pulp paperback market. Her novels reached readers who found little of their lives elsewhere in print.
77702-capital-punishment-among-the-jews:
Capital Punishment Among the Jews, by D De Sola Pool, is a paper read before the New York Board of Jewish Ministers on the history of the death penalty in Jewish law. The Bloch Publishing Company printed it in New York in 1916.

Pool traces the subject from the Bible through Josephus, the rabbinic writings, and the answers of medieval rabbis. Rabbinic law, he notes, knew only four lawful ways of putting a criminal to death: stoning, burning, beheading, and strangulation. Later chapters take up the Jewish attitude toward the penalty itself. Rabbinical softenings, legal limits on the courts, and the gap between practice and theory follow. A final chapter traces the later growth of the law after the Talmud. The study shows a system that kept the penalty on the books while hedged it with safeguards.
7807-georgina-of-the-rainbows:
Annie Fellows Johnston's Georgiana of the Rainbows, set at old Cape Cod, follows a girl through playmate mothers, town criers, green stairs, pirate steps, and spend-the-day guests. A telegram takes Barby away, a birthday prism shines, moving pictures flicker, and an old rifle gives up its secret.

Later chapters bring buried treasure, a narrow escape, a storm, dunes, a liniment wagon, a wild-cat woman, rainbow games, and light dawning for Uncle Darcy. Dedicated to a little goddaughter, Anne Elizabeth, the book mixes seaside adventure with family feeling and a child's bright fancy.
78234-as-the-wind-blows:
Eden Phillpotts gathers lyric poems in a volume issued in 1920 at New York and London. Many pieces turn to Dartmoor, with titles on Eylesbarrow, Rundlestone, Cherrybrook, and the river Dart. Others look outward, to Swinburne, to the grave of Keats, and to Gallipoli.

The opening poem calls the Hesperides to a bare autumn barrow and asks one token of grace for a life stripped by storms. A nocturne follows, set among olive trees and campaniles under a rising moon. Songs of larches, lapwings, hunters, and west winds fill the middle of the book. Readers get Phillpotts in his lyric vein, rooted in moor and stream, with a sad, musical cast that suits his Devon ground.
78614-cows-is-cows:
W C Tuttle wrote Cows Is Cows, a Western tale told in the rough speech of Yellow Rock County. Sheriff Magpie Simpkins stands at the heart of the tale. A tall, thin preacher who calls himself a Bringer of Light walks into the sheriff's office. His full name is Obadiah Ezekiel Moses Brown.

Magpie jokes with the man and turns his talk to work at hand. Rustlers have plagued the county for three days. Stock men blame the sheriff for lax work. Magpie asks the preacher to carry his light to four named men. The humor rests on dry talk, odd looks, and the clash of church speech with ranch life.
79377-the-golliwog-news:
Philip and Fay Inchfawn wrote The Golliwog News, a story of three children and a toy newspaper, first published in London in 1913. Smith drew the illustrations. Gladys, aged ten, owns a big golliwog named John James. He slips from her bed at night and is found on the nursery floor in the morning.

Chapters follow a seaside excursion, a football match, and a dolls' parliament. Birdland City, Fish Town, a banquet, and an exhibition keep the toys busy. A supplement prints the toy newspaper itself. The book reached a fourth edition by 1919. Its verse openings and gentle nonsense belong to a nursery world that modern readers will find very much of its period.
8058-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
Hebrews opens without a greeting, arguing that God, who once spoke through prophets, has now spoken through his Son, heir of all things and brightness of God's glory. The letter presents Jesus as greater than angels, greater than Moses, and the true high priest who offers himself once for all. Its readers, tempted to drift back, are urged to hold fast, warned against falling away, and cheered by the roll of faith in chapter eleven.

Hebrews is the New Testament's most sustained piece of theology, weaving the Old Testament sacrificial system into an argument for Christ. Its language is elevated and its reasoning intricate. In the King James Version, its phrases about faith as the substance of things hoped for have become part of English devotion, and the letter remains essential for understanding early Christian thought.
8285-the-world-english-bible-web-hebrews:
Hebrews is a sermon more than a letter, written to Jewish Christians tempted to drift back to old ways. Its unknown author argues that Jesus surpasses angels, Moses, and the high priests, and that his single sacrifice replaces the repeated offerings of the temple. Long chains of Old Testament quotations build the case, step by step.

The famous chapter on faith then marches through Abel, Abraham, Moses, and others who trusted without seeing the promise fulfilled. It closes with plain calls to endure hardship and care for one another. Hebrews rewards slow reading: dense, poetic, and argued like a lawyer's brief for staying the course.
8846-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Hebrews, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens with God, who in ancient days spoke to forefathers in many distinct messages and by various methods through the prophets. Speaking at the end of these days through a Son, predestined Lord of the universe, through whom he made the ages. The Son brightly reflects God's glory, is the exact representation of his being, upholds the universe by his powerful word. And, after securing purification from sin, sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.

Superior to angels by the name he inherits, the Son becomes the letter's centre. Hebrews argues from priesthood, sacrifice, and covenant that Christ fulfils and surpasses the old order. Weymouth's plain version helps readers follow the letter's long, intricate argument. Hebrews is the New Testament's most theological book, and this volume gives it whole, in modern English that keeps its grandeur without its archaisms.
9314-the-calling-of-dan-matthews:
Harold Bell Wright wrote this novel in 1909 about Dan Matthews, a young minister finding his calling. The story opens in Corinth, with Hope Farwell's ministry, the home of the Ally, and a great day in town. Dan sees the other side, faces tragedy, and learns to save a life, not just preach about one.

Chapters on fishing, common ground, and a laborer and his hire carry Dan from pulpit pride to humble service. Wright, famed for The Shepherd of the Hills, writes plainly and warmly. The novel remains a popular tale of faith tested by real work and real people.
9509-southern-lights-and-shadows:
Southern Lights and Shadows, a Harper's collection from 1907, gathers short tales of the American South. William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited the set, with tales by Grace MacGowan Cooke, Abby Meguire Roach, and Alice MacGowan. The Capture of Andy Proudfoot opens, as a woodsman stalks a man through pine woods. Other tales range from piny woods to mammy's kitchen and a snipe hunt.

Stories include Pap Overholt, The Level of Fortune, and The Courtship of Colonel Bill, each with a Southern voice and scene. Humor, danger, and local color mix in equal parts. A reader gets a vivid sampler of Southern short fiction, told by writers who knew the region's speech and soil.
a-daughter-of-the-snows: Jack London tells of Frona Welse, a daughter of the snows in gold rush Alaska. The novel opens aboard a steamer, where Frona hurries ashore toward a big log house among the pines. Gold rushers crowd the country, and Frona meets their world with spirit and independence. London writes a northern tale of love, courage, and the claims of civilization.
a-merry-dialogue-declaringe-the-properti: Desiderius Erasmus writes a merry dialogue declaring the properties of shrewd shrews and honest wives. Translated into English in 1557, the dialogue is pleasant and profitable in the author's manner. Erasmus, the famous clerk of Rotterdam, stages a debate on marriage. The old spelling of the text is preserved for modern readers.
britannica-1911-agrarian-laws:
Agrarian Laws concern the public land of ancient Rome. Ager publicus was land won by conquest. Republic principle barred free gifts of state property. The people's consent was needed for any disposal. Land could be leased for state revenue instead. Dues were paid by those occupying it. Land could also be assigned to poor citizens. Assignment ended state ownership of the plot. Colonies planted garrisons and relieved poverty at once. Roman speakers linked agrarian law with colonization closely.

Tenure conditions are traced through laws. The Lex Agraria of 111 B.C. reveals African practice. Tax farmers collected dues from possessors there. Caps protected occupiers from overcharging by farmers. Later emperors tried reclaiming unassigned oddments of land. Domitian finally recognized such holdings as private property. The huge entry runs from early Republic to Empire.
britannica-1911-brehon-laws:
Brehon laws is the common English name, though not the strict one, for the old laws of Ireland, called Feineachas in Irish after the Feine, the free Gaelic farming folk. Brehon itself comes from the Gaelic word for a judge. Two grades of law stand out: Cain law, wide in reach and heard only by trained judges, and Urradhus law, handled by nobles and lesser courts.

Surviving copies sit on vellum sheets copied from the 8th to the 13th century and now held in Dublin, London, Oxford and other stores. The greatest book is the Senchus Mor, the Great Old Law Book, though no copy is whole. Old annals date its cleansing and writing to the year 438, in the reign of King Laeghaire. Named law tracts such as the Book of Aicill are traced to early kings and scholars.
britannica-1911-chickasaws:
Chickasaws are a tribe of North American Indians of Muskhogean stock, now settled in the western part of Oklahoma. Their former range was northern Mississippi and parts of Tennessee, and tradition links them closely with the Creeks and Choctaws. They say they crossed the Mississippi with those tribes from the west and settled in what is now north-east Mississippi. De Soto visited them in 1540, and they stayed hostile to the French colonists.

Relations with the English were better, and a treaty with the United States followed in 1786. In 1832 to 1834 the remaining 3,600 gave up 6,442,400 acres and joined the Choctaws, then separated again in 1855 by paying 150,000 dollars. They joined the Confederates in the Civil War and lost ground, then saw their rights restored in 1865. Their own tribal government, with governor, senate and house, virtually ceased in 1906.
britannica-1911-corn-laws:
Corn Laws are the subject of a long entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. In England, laws on corn dealt with trade at home and trade abroad from an early date. Roads were so bad that the home trade chain was weak. Grain could be scarce in one part of the realm and full in the next.

Sea or river trade to a port abroad was in many cases more easy than cart trade at home. Sharp swings in price were thus the norm. The first corn laws grew from that state of things. Their aim was to lower the price of corn. Ship trade out was banned, and grain trade at home had low rank. Rent was then paid in kind, so the king and the lords held vast grain of their own. The entry gives a firm base for the long fight on bread prices.
britannica-1911-fugitive-slave-laws:
Fugitive Slave Laws were United States statutes of 1793 and 1850 for returning escaped slaves to their owners. The duty itself was older: a clause stood in the New England Confederation of 1643, in the Ordinance of 1787 for the Northwest Territory, and in the federal Constitution. The act of February 1793 let judges or magistrates decide a fugitive status finally, with no jury trial.

Northern states answered with Personal Liberty Laws, and the Underground Railroad grew. The harsher act of September 1850, part of the Compromise measures, used special commissioners, barred the fugitive own testimony, and paid the commissioner ten dollars for the claimant and five against. Abuses followed, more liberty laws passed, and Wisconsin court even declared the act void in 1859. The entry names the arrests of Sims, Shadrach, Jerry McHenry, Anthony Burns, and the Garner families as helps toward civil war. The act was repealed in June 1864.
britannica-1911-gallows:
Gallows is the frame used to carry out a death sentence by hanging. The 1911 Britannica entry describes its usual form, two upright posts with a cross-beam, and older forms such as the great stone structure at Montfaucon near Paris. It also notes that Roman crosses were gallows, and that older Bible versions used the word for the cross of Christ.

Modern practice, as the entry gives it, sets the condemned on a platform or drop, used in England from 1760, so the fall breaks the spinal cord. Older methods, a cart drawn away, a ladder, or hauling the man up by a weight, killed by slow choking. The entry then separates the gibbet, a post where dead criminals were hung in chains as a warning, and explains the phrase 'to gibbet' from that custom.
britannica-1911-game-laws:
Game laws in English law are the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The term covers the statutes that govern hunting and taking wild animals. These laws grew out of common-law views on property. Norman kings and feudal lords also prized the chase. At common law a wild animal belongs to no one. It becomes property only when killed or caught.

The article works through the rules with old examples. A bird in the hand is owned, a bird in the bush is not. Bees are not property until they are hived. A swarm that leaves the hive stays the owner's while he can follow it. But he may not chase it onto another man's land. An exception is made for deer and hares hunted with hounds. These rules form the base on which the game statutes rest.
britannica-1911-navigation-laws:
Navigation laws govern how a state controls shipping in its own waters. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats them as local law more than sea law in general. Their base is a state right to guard its own trade. Two broad classes of such laws are set out at the start.

One class sought a trade monopoly for the state that made it. British acts from 1381 onward forced goods into British ships. The chief act of 1660 kept coastal trade for British crews alone. By 1854 most of those limits had lapsed in Britain. The entry then compares the British path with rules in the United States.
britannica-1911-st-andrews:
Saint Andrews, a city and port in Fife, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. Its count in 1901 was 7,621 people. It stands on a bay of the North Sea, on a rock shelf near fifty feet high. Cliffs on its north side hold caves worn by the sea.

Near all life in the town turns on schooling and golf, the piece says. The Royal and Ancient Golf Club, founded in 1754, makes the laws of the game. The town links, gained in 1894, rank among the finest in the world. Crowds come for the game, the sharp air, and the sand beach. Small trades list brewing, tanning, shipping, and fishing.
britannica-1911-sumptuary-laws:
Sumptuary laws are laws meant to limit or rule the private spending of a community's citizens, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces them from ancient Greece. Such laws may spring from political, economic, or moral motives. They flourished most among the Dorian peoples, whose temper was austere.

The entry gives Sparta as the great case: no drinking parties, and no house or furniture made with tools finer than axe and saw. Gold and silver money were banned, iron alone being allowed. Shared public meals, more than any rule, kept Spartan life simple. It also notes strict bans on costly female dress in other Greek cities, and Solon's curbs on dowries, banquets, and funerals at Athens.
britannica-1911-taylor-philip-meadows:
Taylor, Philip Meadows is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Anglo-Indian officer and novelist. He was born at Liverpool on the twenty-fifth of September 1808 and died in 1876. At fifteen he sailed to India as a clerk to a Bombay merchant. That house was in money trouble when he arrived.

In 1824 he took a commission in the service of the nizam, and he stayed loyal to that service all his career. He soon moved from soldiering to civil work. In that work he learned the tongues and ways of southern India as few men have. He was in turn judge, engineer, artist, and writer. On leave in England in 1840 he brought out his first Indian novel, Confessions of a Thug.
britannica-1911-welsh-laws:
Welsh laws, or Leges Walliae, form the old legal code of Wales. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits King Howel Dda, who died in 950, as its maker. A preface tells how Howel called clergy and nobles to review the laws. Thirteen chosen men were tasked to keep, explain, and cut rules as needed.

Three copies were made for courts at different seats in Wales. Bishops cursed any who broke the confirmed code in that tale. Three versions of the code survive for north, south, and north east Wales. Manuscripts differ widely and hold later additions, the entry warns. Latin versions of the Welsh text are also very old.
britannica-1911-yaws:
Yaws is a catching tropical disease known by many local names. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica maps its spread and sores. West Indian speech gave it the name in English use. In Brazil it is boba, in Fiji coko, in Ceylon parangi.

A French name likens its growths to a raspberry fruit. For years men thought it a disease of Africans alone. The same sickness was found old among Malays in the East Indies. It runs a long slow course with skin eruption. Small pimples rise, grow, and break into thick discharge. A red fungous lump then shows beneath a whitish slough. Face, neck, armpits, and groin are its favored seats. Hair at a sore spot turns white as it heals or spreads.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptismal-vow:
Baptismal vows are the popular name for renunciations made by an adult just before baptism, or by sponsors for infants. They lack the theological weight of vows properly so called. The Roman Ritual asks three questions, each pressing whether the person renounces Satan, his works, and his pomps. To each, the person or sponsor answers, 'I do renounce.'

The practice reaches back to organized Christian worship's beginnings, upheld by Tertullian and St Basil as venerable tradition. Basil traces it to the Apostles, though Scripture does not explicitly warrant it. The Apostolic Constitutions give a fuller form, renouncing Satan, his works, pomps, worship, angels, and inventions. The candidate then turns east, toward light, and pledges himself to Christ, to be ruled by his precepts. Renewal of these promises is widespread at missions, First Communions, and Confirmations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-to-th:
The Epistle to the Hebrews is treated under argument, doctrine, style, readers, author, circumstances, and importance. In the oldest Greek manuscripts it follows the letters to the churches and precedes the pastoral letters. Later copies place it last among Paul's epistles. It opens without Paul's usual introduction, announcing the superiority of the Son's revelation over the prophets'.

From Scripture it proves the New Covenant's superiority over the Old. The Son stands above angels as mediators of the Old Covenant, above Moses and Joshua as its founders, and Christ's priesthood after Melchisedech above the Levitical priesthood after Aaron. Doctrinal statements are broken again and again by practical exhortations to hold fast to the faith and not slip back into Mosaic worship. The second part repeats calls to steadfast faith and Christian living, closing with personal remarks and a greeting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th:
